items.bodyEn: Kameyama was a castle town: the Tōkaidō climbed steeply to the Kyōguchi gate of Kameyama Castle, seat of the Ishikawa lords in the late Edo period. Hiroshige painted that slope in his print Kameyama: Clear Weather after Snow, a lord's procession toiling uphill under a sky swept clean. The 1843 survey counted one honjin and twenty-one inns.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Hōeidō Tōkaidō (c. 1833), 'Kameyama: Yukibare'; 東海道宿村大概帳 (1843)

items.bodyEn: 急がば回れ, when in a hurry, go around, began as a Tōkaidō travel tip. A poem attributed to the renga master Sōchō warns that the Yabase ferry across Lake Biwa is quick but risky in the winds off Mount Hiei, so a hurried traveler should take the long bridge at Seta instead. The safe detour beat the risky shortcut.
items.sourceNote: Kōjien (Iwanami), entry 急がば回れ; poem by Sōchō recorded in Seisuishō (醒睡笑, 1623)

items.bodyEn: Many idioms at this station put feeling in the 腹, the belly. 腹が立つ is to get angry, 腹を割って話す is to speak frankly, 腹を括る is to brace yourself. Mind the particles: in 腹が立つ the belly rises on its own, so が; to make it rise on purpose you say 腹を立てる with the transitive verb.

The 亀 of 亀山 is a picture. Its old form 龜 shows a turtle from the side: head at the top, shell with legs sticking out in the middle, tail at the bottom. The Shuowen Jiezi describes it as depicting legs, shell and tail. Japan's simplified 亀 keeps the head and the ribbed shell. Readings: かめ and キ.
items.sourceNote: Shuowen Jiezi (説文解字), entry 龜: 象足甲尾之形; Kanjigen (Gakken)
